claim: Two-stage learning has been described in hippocampal memory consolidation, where recent memories dependent on the hippocampus are transferred to the neocortex for long-term storage.
source: During hippocampal memory consolidation, recent memories, that are dependent on the hippocampus, are transferred to the neocortex for long-term storage (Frankland and Bontempi, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Frankland and Bontempi, 2005

claim: The rat motor cortex provides essential input to sub-cortical circuits during skill learning, but then becomes dispensable for executing certain skills.
source: Similarly, the rat motor cortex provides essential input to sub-cortical circuits during skill learning, but then becomes dispensable for executing certain skills (Kawai et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kawai et al., 2015

claim: A paradigmatic example of two-stage learning occurs in songbirds learning their courtship songs.
source: A paradigmatic example of two-stage learning occurs in songbirds learning their courtship songs (Andalman and Fee, 2009; Turner and Desmurget, 2010; Warren et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Andalman and Fee, 2009; Turner and Desmurget, 2010; Warren et al., 2011

claim: Zebra finches learn their song from their fathers as juveniles and keep the same song for life.
source: Zebra finches, commonly used in birdsong research, learn their song from their fathers as juveniles, and keep the same song for life (Immelmann, 1969).
evidence: Supported by citation to Immelmann, 1969

claim: HVC projection neurons fire sparse spike bursts in precise synchrony with the song.
source: Area HVC is a timebase circuit, with projection neurons that fire sparse spike bursts in precise synchrony with the song (Hahnloser et al., 2002; Lynch et al., 2016; Picardo et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hahnloser et al., 2002; Lynch et al., 2016; Picardo et al., 2016

claim: A population of neurons from HVC projects to the robust nucleus of the arcopallium (RA), a pre-motor area, which then projects to motor neurons controlling respiratory and syringeal muscles.
source: A population of neurons from HVC projects to the robust nucleus of the arcopallium (RA), a pre-motor area, which then projects to motor neurons controlling respiratory and syringeal muscles (Leonardo and Fee, 2005; Simpson and Vicario, 1990; Yu and Margoliash, 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to Leonardo and Fee, 2005; Simpson and Vicario, 1990; Yu and Margoliash, 1996

claim: LMAN spiking is highly variable across different renditions of the song.
source: Unlike HVC and RA activity patterns, LMAN spiking is highly variable across different renditions of the song (Kao et al., 2008; Ölveczky et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kao et al., 2008; Ölveczky et al., 2005

claim: LMAN is the output of the anterior forebrain pathway, a circuit involving the song-specialized basal ganglia.
source: LMAN is the output of the anterior forebrain pathway, a circuit involving the song-specialized basal ganglia (Perkel, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Perkel, 2004

claim: It was thought that LMAN's role was simply to inject variability into the song because of the variability in its activity patterns.
source: Because of the variability in its activity patterns, it was thought that LMAN's role was simply to inject variability into the song (Ölveczky et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ölveczky et al., 2005

claim: Prior models treated LMAN as a pure Poisson noise generator and assumed that a reward signal is received directly in RA.
source: For this reason, prior models tended to treat LMAN as a pure Poisson noise generator, and assume that a reward signal is received directly in RA (Fiete et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fiete et al., 2007

claim: The reward signal reaches Area X, the song-specialized basal ganglia, rather than RA.
source: More recent evidence, however, suggests that the reward signal reaches Area X, the song-specialized basal ganglia, rather than RA (Gadagkar et al., 2016; Hoffmann et al., 2016; Kubikova et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gadagkar et al., 2016; Hoffmann et al., 2016; Kubikova et al., 2010

claim: LMAN firing patterns contain a corrective bias guiding plasticity in RA.
source: Taken together with the fact that LMAN firing patterns are not uniformly random, but rather contain a corrective bias guiding plasticity in RA (Andalman and Fee, 2009; Warren et al., 2011), this suggests that we should rethink our models of song acquisition.
evidence: Supported by citations to Andalman and Fee, 2009; Warren et al., 2011

claim: The model reproduces the observed changes in the spiking statistics of RA neurons as juvenile birds learn their song.
source: Applied to the vocal control circuit of songbirds, our model reproduces the observed changes in the spiking statistics of RA neurons as juvenile birds learn their song.
evidence: Stated as a result of the model in the Introduction

claim: The model predicts how the LMAN signal should be adapted to properties of RA synapses.
source: Our framework also predicts how the LMAN signal should be adapted to properties of RA synapses. This prediction can be tested in future experiments.
evidence: Stated as a prediction from the model

claim: A simple reinforcement learning algorithm suffices to implement the learning rule proposed in the model.
source: We nevertheless demonstrate that a simple reinforcement learning algorithm suffices to implement the learning rule we propose.
evidence: Stated as a demonstration from the model

claim: The conductor provides input to the student in the form of temporally precise patterns.
source: The conductor provides input to the student in the form of temporally precise patterns.
evidence: Description of the model architecture

claim: The goal of learning is for the student to convert conductor input to a predefined output pattern.
source: The goal of learning is for the student to convert this input to a predefined output pattern.
evidence: Description of the model objective

claim: The tutor provides a signal that guides plasticity at the conductor–student synapses.
source: The tutor provides a signal that guides plasticity at the conductor–student synapses.
evidence: Description of the model architecture

claim: In the songbird model, the conductor is HVC, the student is RA, and the tutor is LMAN.
source: Relating this to the songbird, the conductor is HVC, the student is RA, and the tutor is LMAN.
evidence: Explicit mapping between model components and brain regions

claim: The song can be viewed as a mapping between clock-like HVC activity patterns and muscle-related RA outputs.
source: The song can be viewed as a mapping between clock-like HVC activity patterns and muscle-related RA outputs.
evidence: Conceptual description of the birdsong system

claim: If the tutor only has access to a scalar representation of how successful the student rendition is, it needs to solve the credit assignment problem.
source: More realistically, the tutor might only have access to a scalar representation of how successful the student rendition of the desired output is, perhaps in the form of a reward signal. A tutor in this case has to solve the so-called 'credit assignment problem'—it needs to identify which student neurons are responsible for the reward.
evidence: Logical reasoning about the tutor's computational challenge

claim: A standard way to solve the credit assignment problem is to inject variability in the student output and reinforce the firing of neurons that precede reward.
source: A standard way to achieve this is to inject variability in the student output and reinforce the firing of neurons that precede reward (see for example (Fiete et al., 2007) in the birdsong context).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fiete et al., 2007 and general knowledge

claim: In the model, the tutor has a dual role of providing both an instructive signal and variability.
source: Thus, in our model, the tutor has a dual role of providing both an instructive signal and variability, as in birdsong.
evidence: Description of the model design

claim: The guiding signals for each RA neuron come from several LMAN neurons in the songbird.
source: in the songbird, the guiding signals for each RA neuron come from several LMAN neurons (Canady et al., 1988; Garst-Orozco et al., 2014; Herrmann and Arnold, 1991).
evidence: Supported by citations to Canady et al., 1988; Garst-Orozco et al., 2014; Herrmann and Arnold, 1991

claim: In the model, the net input from the tutor to each student neuron is summarized as a single function.
source: In our model, we summarized the net input from the tutor to the jth student neuron as a single function gj⁢(t).
evidence: Description of model simplification

claim: Many different forms of hetero-synaptic plasticity have been observed.
source: Many different forms of such hetero-synaptic plasticity have been observed.
evidence: General statement about experimental observations

claim: In rate-based synaptic plasticity, high tutor firing rates lead to synaptic potentiation and low tutor firing rates lead to depression.
source: For example, in rate-based synaptic plasticity high tutor firing rates lead to synaptic potentiation and low tutor firing rates lead to depression (Chistiakova and Volgushev, 2009; Chistiakova et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chistiakova and Volgushev, 2009; Chistiakova et al., 2014

claim: Mehaffey and Doupe (2015) measured a timing-dependent plasticity rule in slices of zebra finch RA where the relative arrival times of spike bursts from different input pathways set the sign of synaptic change.
source: In timing-dependent rules, such as the one recently measured by Mehaffey and Doupe (2015) in slices of zebra finch RA (see Figure 1C), the relative arrival times of spike bursts from different input pathways set the sign of synaptic change.
evidence: Supported by citation to Mehaffey and Doupe, 2015 and reference to Figure 1C

claim: Motor learning with a heterosynaptic plasticity rule requires convolving the motor error with a kernel whose timescale is related to the structure of the plasticity rule.
source: In short, motor learning with a heterosynaptic plasticity rule requires convolving the motor error with a kernel whose timescale is related to the structure of the plasticity rule, but is otherwise independent of the motor program.
evidence: Summary of mathematical derivation

claim: A mismatched tutor should slow or disrupt convergence to the desired output.
source: A mismatched tutor should slow or disrupt convergence to the desired output.
evidence: Prediction from the model

claim: The student output rapidly converged to the target with a matched tutor when the sign of plasticity is determined by the tutor's firing rate.
source: Figure 3A and online Video 1 show convergence with a matched tutor when the sign of plasticity is determined by the tutor's firing rate. We see that the student output rapidly converged to the target.
evidence: Shown in simulation results in Figure 3A and Video 1

claim: The student converged steadily to the desired output with a matched tutor when the sign of plasticity is largely determined by the relative timing of the tutor signal and the student output, but at a somewhat slower rate than with rate-based plasticity.
source: Figure 3B and online Video 2 show convergence with a matched tutor when the sign of plasticity is largely determined by the relative timing of the tutor signal and the student output. We see again that the student converged steadily to the desired output, but at a somewhat slower rate than in Figure 3A.
evidence: Shown in simulation results in Figure 3B and Video 2

claim: Learning slowed down when a firing rate constraint was imposed on the tutor, but the accuracy of the final rendition was not affected.
source: Learning slowed down with this change (Figure 4A and online Video 3) as a result of the tutor firing rates saturating when the mismatch between the motor output and the target output was large. However, the accuracy of the final rendition was not affected by saturation in the tutor (Figure 4A, inset).
evidence: Shown in simulation results in Figure 4A and Video 3

claim: Sequential learning occurred when the firing rate constraint was imposed on a matched tutor with a long memory timescale, where early features in the output were learned first before later features were addressed.
source: In the extreme case of very long integration timescales, learning became sequential: early features in the output were learned first, before later features were addressed, as in Figure 4B and online Video 4.
evidence: Shown in simulation results in Figure 4B and Video 4

claim: The sequential learning observed in the model is reminiscent of the learning rule described in Memmesheimer et al. (2014).
source: This is reminiscent of the learning rule described in (Memmesheimer et al., 2014).
evidence: Comparison to prior work cited

claim: For efficient learning to occur with nonlinearities in student neurons, the synaptic plasticity rule should depend not just on the tutor and conductor, but also on the activity of the postsynaptic student neurons.
source: The key result is that for efficient learning to occur, the synaptic plasticity rule should depend not just on the tutor and conductor, but also on the activity of the postsynaptic student neurons (details in Appendix).
evidence: Result from model extension described in the text

claim: Dependence of plasticity on postsynaptic activity is commonly seen in experiments.
source: Such dependence on postsynaptic activity is commonly seen in experiments (Chistiakova and Volgushev, 2009; Chistiakova et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chistiakova and Volgushev, 2009; Chistiakova et al., 2014

claim: The model continues to work with biologically realistic synapses that cannot change sign from excitatory to inhibitory during learning.
source: This shows that our model continues to work with biologically realistic synapses that cannot change sign from excitatory to inhibitory during learning.
evidence: Conclusion from testing the rectification constraint

claim: Juvenile songbirds produce a 'babble' that converges through learning to an adult song strongly resembling the tutor song.
source: Juvenile songbirds produce a 'babble' that converges through learning to an adult song strongly resembling the tutor song.
evidence: General knowledge about birdsong development

claim: Song-aligned spiking patterns in pre-motor area RA become more stereotyped and cluster in shorter, better-defined bursts as the bird matures.
source: This is reflected in the song-aligned spiking patterns in pre-motor area RA, which become more stereotyped and cluster in shorter, better-defined bursts as the bird matures (Figure 5A).
evidence: Shown in experimental data in Figure 5A

claim: The model could reproduce key statistics of spiking in RA over the course of song learning.
source: We tested whether our model could reproduce key statistics of spiking in RA over the course of song learning.
evidence: Stated as a test of the model

claim: Each HVC neuron fires one short, precisely timed burst of 5–6 spikes at a single moment in the motor program, following the experiments of Hahnloser et al. (2002).
source: Following the experiments of Hahnloser et al. (2002), we modeled each neuron in HVC (the conductor) as firing one short, precisely timed burst of 5–6 spikes at a single moment in the motor program.
evidence: Model design based on citation to Hahnloser et al., 2002

claim: LMAN neurons have highly variable firing patterns that facilitate experimentation but also contain a corrective bias.
source: LMAN (tutor) neurons are known to have highly variable firing patterns that facilitate experimentation, but also contain a corrective bias (Andalman and Fee, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Andalman and Fee, 2009

claim: LMAN was modeled as producing inhomogeneous Poisson spike trains with a time-dependent firing rate.
source: Thus we modeled LMAN as producing inhomogeneous Poisson spike trains with a time-dependent firing rate given by Equation (5) in our model.
evidence: Description of model implementation

claim: The LMAN-RA synapses were modeled as a mixture of AMPA and NMDA receptors, following the songbird data.
source: The LMAN-RA synapses were modeled in a current-based approach as a mixture of AMPA and NMDA receptors, following the songbird data (Garst-Orozco et al., 2014; Stark and Perkel, 1999).
evidence: Model design based on citations to Garst-Orozco et al., 2014; Stark and Perkel, 1999

claim: The initial weights for all synapses were tuned to produce RA firing patterns resembling juvenile birds, subject to constraints from direct measurements in slice recordings.
source: The initial weights for all synapses were tuned to produce RA firing patterns resembling juvenile birds (Ölveczky et al., 2011), subject to constraints from direct measurements in slice recordings (Garst-Orozco et al., 2014) (see Materials and methods for details, and Figure 5B for a comparison between neural recordings and spiking in our model).
evidence: Model design based on citations to Ölveczky et al., 2011 and Garst-Orozco et al., 2014, with comparison shown in Figure 5B

claim: Learning proceeded effectively in the spiking model when the tutor error integration timescale and the student plasticity rule were matched, as long as the tutor error integration timescale was not too large.
source: As long as the tutor error integration timescale was not too large, learning proceeded effectively when the tutor error integration timescale and the student plasticity rule were matched (see Figure 5C and online Video 5), with mismatches slowing down or abolishing learning, just as in our rate-based study (compare Figure 5D with Figure 3C).
evidence: Shown in simulation results in Figure 5C, 5D, and Video 5

claim: The rate of learning and the accuracy of the trained state were lower in the spiking model compared to the rate-based model.
source: The rate of learning and the accuracy of the trained state were lower in the spiking model compared to the rate-based model.
evidence: Comparison between model variants

claim: The lower accuracy in the spiking model arises because the tutor neurons fire stochastically, unlike the deterministic neurons used in the rate-based simulations.
source: The lower accuracy arises because the tutor neurons fire stochastically, unlike the deterministic neurons used in the rate-based simulations.
evidence: Explanation for observed difference between models

claim: Fluctuations in the conductor–student weights lead to some weights getting clamped at 0 due to the positivity constraint, which leads to the motor program overshooting the target.
source: and (2) the fluctuations in the conductor–student weights lead to some weights getting clamped at 0 due to the positivity constraint, which leads to the motor program overshooting the target (see Appendix).
evidence: Explanation provided with reference to Appendix

claim: Spiking in the model tends to be a little more regular than that in the recordings.
source: Spiking in our model tends to be a little more regular than that in the recordings (compare Figure 5A and Figure 5B).
evidence: Comparison between model and experimental data in Figures 5A and 5B

claim: The greater regularity in model spiking could be due to sources of noise present in the brain which were not modeled.
source: This could be due to sources of noise that are present in the brain which we did not model.
evidence: Speculation about model limitations

claim: Many LMAN spikes occur in bursts in reality, while in the simulation LMAN firing is Poisson.
source: One detail that our model does not capture is the fact that many LMAN spikes occur in bursts, while in our simulation LMAN firing is Poisson.
evidence: Acknowledgment of model limitation

claim: Bursts are more likely to produce spikes in downstream RA neurons particularly because of the NMDA dynamics, and thus a bursty LMAN will be more effective at injecting variability into RA.
source: Bursts are more likely to produce spikes in downstream RA neurons particularly because of the NMDA dynamics, and thus a bursty LMAN will be more effective at injecting variability into RA (Kojima et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kojima et al., 2013

claim: Small inaccuracies in aligning the recorded spikes to the song are likely to contribute apparent variability between renditions in experiments.
source: Small inaccuracies in aligning the recorded spikes to the song are also likely to contribute apparent variability between renditions in experiments.
evidence: Speculation about experimental limitations

claim: Learning is robust to credit mis-assignment even for fairly large values of the error fraction up to about 40%, but quickly deteriorates as this fraction approaches 50%.
source: Figure 6A shows that learning is robust to this kind of mis-assignment even for fairly large values of the error fraction ρ up to about 40%, but quickly deteriorates as this fraction approaches 50%.
evidence: Shown in simulation results in Figure 6A

claim: Due to environmental factors that affect development of different individuals in different ways, it is unlikely that the student–output mapping can be innate.
source: Due to environmental factors that affect development of different individuals in different ways, it is unlikely that the student–output mapping can be innate.
evidence: Reasoning about biological constraints

claim: The tutor circuit must learn the student–output mapping.
source: As such, the tutor circuit must learn the mapping.
evidence: Logical consequence of the previous claim

claim: LMAN in the bird receives an indirect evaluation signal via Area X, which might be used to effect learning of the student–output mapping.
source: Indeed, it is known that LMAN in the bird receives an indirect evaluation signal via Area X, which might be used to effect this learning (Andalman and Fee, 2009; Gadagkar et al., 2016; Hoffmann et al., 2016; Kubikova et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Andalman and Fee, 2009; Gadagkar et al., 2016; Hoffmann et al., 2016; Kubikova et al., 2010

claim: Learning with the reinforcement strategy converges to an accurate rendition of the target output.
source: To test our learning rule, we ran simulations using this reinforcement strategy and found that learning again converges to an accurate rendition of the target output (Figure 6B, inset and online Video 6).
evidence: Shown in simulation results in Figure 6B and Video 6

claim: The number of repetitions needed for training with reinforcement learning is greatly increased compared to the case in which the credit assignment is assumed known by the tutor circuit.
source: The number of repetitions needed for training is greatly increased compared to the case in which the credit assignment is assumed known by the tutor circuit (compare Figure 6B to Figure 5C).
evidence: Comparison between simulation results in Figures 6B and 5C

claim: The motor output in reward-based simulations tends to initially overshoot the target because of the extra training time needed for the tutor to adapt its signal.
source: Because of the extra training time needed for the tutor to adapt its signal, the motor output in our reward-based simulations tends to initially overshoot the target (leading to the kink in the error at around 2000 repetitions in Figure 6B).
evidence: Observation from simulation results in Figure 6B

claim: The subsequent reduction in output that leads to convergence of the motor program, combined with the positivity constraint on the synaptic strengths, leads to many conductor–student connections being pruned.
source: Interestingly, the subsequent reduction in output that leads to convergence of the motor program, combined with the positivity constraint on the synaptic strengths, leads to many conductor–student connections being pruned (Figure 6D).
evidence: Shown in simulation results in Figure 6D

claim: The pruning of connections in the model mirrors experiments on songbirds, where the number of connections between HVC and RA first increases with learning and then decreases.
source: This mirrors experiments on songbirds, where the number of connections between HVC and RA first increases with learning and then decreases (Garst-Orozco et al., 2014).
evidence: Comparison to experimental data cited from Garst-Orozco et al., 2014

claim: The reinforcement rules proposed are related to the learning rules from Fiete and Seung (2006), Fiete et al. (2007), and Farries and Fairhall (2007).
source: The reinforcement rules proposed here are related to the learning rules from (Fiete and Seung, 2006; Fiete et al., 2007) and (Farries and Fairhall, 2007).
evidence: Comparison to prior work

claim: Previous models focused on learning in a single pass, instead of the two-stage architecture studied here.
source: However, those models focused on learning in a single pass, instead of the two-stage architecture that we studied.
evidence: Comparison to prior work

claim: In Fiete et al. (2007), area LMAN was assumed to generate pure Poisson noise and reinforcement learning took place at the HVC–RA synapses.
source: In particular, in Fiete et al. (2007), area LMAN was assumed to generate pure Poisson noise and reinforcement learning took place at the HVC–RA synapses.
evidence: Description of prior work cited

claim: In the current model, which is in better agreement with recent evidence regarding the roles of RA and LMAN in birdsong, reinforcement learning first takes place in the anterior forebrain pathway (AFP), for which LMAN is the output.
source: In our model, which is in better agreement with recent evidence regarding the roles of RA and LMAN in birdsong (Andalman and Fee, 2009), reinforcement learning first takes place in the anterior forebrain pathway (AFP), for which LMAN is the output.
evidence: Description of model design with citation to Andalman and Fee, 2009

claim: A reward-independent heterosynaptic plasticity rule solidifies the information in RA.
source: A reward-independent heterosynaptic plasticity rule then solidifies the information in RA.
evidence: Description of model mechanism

claim: There are indirect projections from HVC to LMAN in the songbird, going through the basal ganglia (Area X) and the dorso-lateral division of the medial thalamus (DLM) in the anterior forebrain pathway.
source: In fact, in the songbird, there are indirect projections from HVC to LMAN, going through the basal ganglia (Area X) and the dorso-lateral division of the medial thalamus (DLM) in the anterior forebrain pathway (Figure 1A) (Perkel, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Perkel, 2004 and shown in Figure 1A

claim: The synapses in the indirect HVC-LMAN pathway could store the required time-dependence of the tutor firing rates.
source: These synapses could store the required time-dependence of the tutor firing rates.
evidence: Speculation about biological implementation

claim: The same synapses in the indirect HVC-LMAN pathway can provide the timebase input that would ensure synchrony between LMAN firing and RA output, as necessary for learning.
source: In addition, the same synapses can provide the timebase input that would ensure synchrony between LMAN firing and RA output, as necessary for learning.
evidence: Speculation about biological implementation

claim: The reinforcement learning rule for the tutor area can be viewed as an effective model for plasticity in the projections between HVC, Area X, DLM, and LMAN.
source: Our reinforcement learning rule for the tutor area, Equation (6), can be viewed as an effective model for plasticity in the projections between HVC, Area X, DLM, and LMAN, as in Fee and Goldberg (2011).
evidence: Interpretation of the model with citation to Fee and Goldberg, 2011

claim: The indirect HVC–LMAN connections behave somewhat like the 'hedonistic synapses' from Seung (2003), though a simpler synaptic model is used here.
source: In this picture, the indirect HVC–LMAN connections behave somewhat like the 'hedonistic synapses' from Seung (2003), though we use a simpler synaptic model here.
evidence: Comparison to prior work cited from Seung, 2003

claim: If the birdsong system supports efficient learning, the model can predict the temporal structure of the firing patterns of RA-projecting LMAN neurons, given the plasticity rule implemented at the HVC–RA synapses.
source: If the birdsong system supports efficient learning, our model can predict the temporal structure of the firing patterns of RA-projecting LMAN neurons, given the plasticity rule implemented at the HVC–RA synapses.
evidence: Prediction from the model

claim: These predictions can be directly tested by recordings from LMAN neurons in singing birds, assuming that a good measure of motor error is available, and that we can estimate how the neurons contribute to this error.
source: These predictions can be directly tested by recordings from LMAN neurons in singing birds, assuming that a good measure of motor error is available, and that we can estimate how the neurons contribute to this error.
evidence: Proposed experimental test

claim: Recordings from a tutor circuit could be combined with a measure of motor error to infer the plasticity rule in a downstream student circuit.
source: Moreover, recordings from a tutor circuit, such as LMAN, could be combined with a measure of motor error to infer the plasticity rule in a downstream student circuit, such as RA.
evidence: Proposed experimental approach

claim: Knowledge of the student plasticity rule could be used to predict the time-dependence of tutor firing rates.
source: Conversely, knowledge of the student plasticity rule could be used to predict the time-dependence of tutor firing rates.
evidence: Proposed experimental approach

claim: According to the model, the firing rate should reflect the integral of the motor error with the timescale predicted by the model.
source: According to our model, the firing rate should reflect the integral of the motor error with the timescale predicted by the model.
evidence: Prediction from the model

claim: If the tutor signal is delivered appropriately in conjunction with a particular syllable, then the premotor bias produced by the stimulation should become incorporated into the motor pathway faster when the timescale of the artificial LMAN signal is properly matched to the RA synaptic plasticity rule.
source: We would predict that if the tutor signal is delivered appropriately (e.g., in conjunction with a particular syllable [Tumer and Brainard, 2007]), then the premotor bias produced by the stimulation should become incorporated into the motor pathway faster when the timescale of the artificial LMAN signal is properly matched to the RA synaptic plasticity rule.
evidence: Prediction from the model with citation to Tumer and Brainard, 2007

claim: The model can be applied more generally to other systems in the brain exhibiting two-stage learning, such as motor learning in mammals.
source: Our model can be applied more generally to other systems in the brain exhibiting two-stage learning, such as motor learning in mammals.
evidence: Proposed generalization of the model

claim: If the plasticity mechanisms in other systems are different from those in songbirds, the predictions for the structure of the guiding signal will vary correspondingly.
source: If the plasticity mechanisms in these systems are different from those in songbirds, our predictions for the structure of the guiding signal will vary correspondingly.

source: It is worth pointing out that our model was derived assuming a certain hierarchy among the timescales that model the student plasticity and the tutor signal. A mismatch between the model predictions and observations could also imply a breakdown of these approximations, rather than failure of the hypothesis that the particular system under study evolved to support efficient learning.

claim: The model is best seen as a mechanism for learning song syllables when applied to birdsong.
source: Applied to birdsong, our model is best seen as a mechanism for learning song syllables.

source: The ordering of syllables in song motifs seems to have a second level of control within HVC and perhaps beyond (Basista et al., 2014; Hamaguchi et al., 2016).

claim: Songs can be distorted by warping their timebase through changes in HVC firing without alterations of the HVC–RA connectivity.
source: Songs can also be distorted by warping their timebase through changes in HVC firing without alterations of the HVC–RA connectivity (Ali et al., 2013).

claim: Recurrent inhibition is present in area RA of the bird.

claim: The initial connectivity between conductor and student neurons was chosen to be sparse.
source: The initial connectivity between conductor and student neurons was chosen to be sparse (see Table 1).

source: The initial distribution of synaptic weights was log-normal, matching experimentally measured values for zebra finches (Garst-Orozco et al., 2014).

claim: Since measurements of HVC synapses per RA neuron are done in the slice, the absolute number is likely to have been underestimated.
source: Since these measurements are done in the slice, the absolute number of HVC synapses per RA neuron is likely to have been underestimated.
evidence: Reasoning about experimental limitations

claim: The number of conductor–student synapses in the simulations is chosen to be higher than the value reported in Garst-Orozco et al. (2014), and is allowed to change during learning.
source: The number of conductor–student synapses we start with in our simulations is thus chosen to be higher than the value reported in that paper (see Table 1), and is allowed to change during learning.
evidence: Description of model implementation

claim: The learning paradigm described is robust to substantial changes in the parameters.
source: We checked that the learning paradigm described here is robust to substantial changes in these parameters, but we have chosen values that are faithful to birdsong experiments and which are thus able to imitate the RA spiking statistics during song.
evidence: Tested in simulations

claim: The synapses projecting onto each student neuron from the tutor have a weight that is fixed during the simulations, reflecting the finding that the average strength of LMAN–RA synapses for zebra finches does not change with age.
source: The synapses projecting onto each student neuron from the tutor have a weight that is fixed during our simulations reflecting the finding in Garst-Orozco et al. (2014) that the average strength of LMAN–RA synapses for zebra finches does not change with age.
evidence: Model design based on citation to Garst-Orozco et al., 2014

claim: There is some evidence that individual LMAN–RA synapses undergo plasticity concurrently with the HVC–RA synapses.
source: There is some evidence that individual LMAN–RA synapses undergo plasticity concurrently with the HVC–RA synapses (Mehaffey and Doupe, 2015) but we did not seek to model this effect.
evidence: Supported by citation to Mehaffey and Doupe, 2015

claim: There are developmental changes in the kinetics of NMDA-mediated synaptic currents in both HVC–RA and LMAN–RA synapses which are not modeled.
source: There are also developmental changes in the kinetics of NMDA-mediated synaptic currents in both HVC–RA and LMAN–RA synapses which we do not model (Stark and Perkel, 1999).
evidence: Acknowledgment of model limitation with citation to Stark and Perkel, 1999

claim: Developmental changes in NMDA kinetics happen early in development, and thus are unlikely to have an effect on song crystallization.
source: These, however, happen early in development, and thus are unlikely to have an effect on song crystallization, which is what our model focuses on.
evidence: Reasoning about the relevance of the omitted effect

claim: Stark and Perkel (1999) observed changes in the relative contribution of NMDA to AMPA responses in the HVC–RA synapses.
source: Stark and Perkel, 1999 also observed changes in the relative contribution of NMDA to AMPA responses in the HVC–RA synapses.
evidence: Description of findings from cited work

claim: There is evidence that area HVC can also contribute to learning, in particular in relation to the temporal structure of song.
source: However, this is an interesting avenue for future work, especially since there is evidence that area HVC can also contribute to learning, in particular in relation to the temporal structure of song (Ali et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ali et al., 2013
